description: I'm an IGCSE student passionate about physics, aerospace, and space exploration. I work with Unreal Engine 5 on game development, world-building, and systems design. I enjoy scientific research, creative problem-solving, and connecting ideas. I'm joining Flame in Freefall to apply my skills to a real-world challenge. I'm looking for teammates interested in coding, Python, research, data analysis, or visualisation. Curiosity, teamwork, and a willingness to learn are what matter most.
summary:
Flare AI is a website that turns NASA's microgravity fire experiments into answers that mission planners, students and engineers can verify. It unifies all 24 combustion investigations in NASA's Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI) repository and 537 individual test records from BASS, BASS-II, FLEX and Saffire. Every record cites the exact NASA table, row or report page it came from, and each one was checked twice: automatically against NASA's own files, and by hand by our team.

Users can rank investigations for a spacecraft, a Moon base or a Mars base; compare experiments like with like; enter conditions such as oxygen level and pressure to find the closest real NASA tests; and ask questions in plain English, answered only from NASA's records.

Flare AI never invents numbers, never pools experiments measured differently, and states plainly when the data is insufficient. This matters: the Moon-base atmosphere in the challenge lies beyond every solid-material test in the data, and NASA's BASS-II report shows materials can burn in microgravity at lower oxygen levels than on Earth.
details:
What it does

We built Flare AI because NASA has run hundreds of fire experiments in space, but the results are spread across reports, spreadsheets and data files that are hard to search or compare. We wanted one place where you can look up what NASA actually tested and see exactly where each number came from.

The site covers all 24 combustion investigations in NASA's PSI repository and 537 individual test records from BASS, BASS-II, FLEX and Saffire. You can:

- rank the investigations for a spacecraft, a Moon base or a Mars base (the scoring rule is printed on the page)

- search and filter every test record, with a link to the NASA table, row or report page it came from

- compare tests side by side, as long as they were measured the same way

- type in an oxygen level and pressure and see the closest real NASA tests

- ask a question in plain English and get an answer that cites NASA's records

- read about real space fires like Apollo 1 and Mir, with NASA's own words kept separate from ours

How it works

We wrote Python scripts that download NASA's data files and the BASS-II report, pull out the test tables, and check them against the originals every time the site is rebuilt. All 126 BASS-II records match NASA's PDF exactly. In 3 cases NASA's spreadsheet and report disagree, so we show both values instead of picking one. After the automated checks, two of us went through all 537 records by hand against NASA's sources.

The website itself is plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, so it loads fast and even works offline. The question-answering part runs on a Netlify server function using Google's Gemini API. It only answers from our NASA records, and if a citation doesn't match a real record, our code throws that point out.

Why it matters

The challenge asks about fire safety for future Moon and Mars habitats. When we looked at the data, we found that the Moon-base atmosphere in the challenge (30% oxygen or more at low pressure) is beyond anything NASA tested with solid materials, and there are no partial-gravity tests at all. We think showing those gaps clearly is as useful as showing the results, because it tells researchers what still needs testing.

One finding that stood out to us: NASA's BASS-II report shows a material kept burning at 13.5% oxygen in microgravity, below the 15.4% limit seen on Earth. Something that passes a fire test on the ground might still burn in a spacecraft.

What we were careful about

We decided early that Flare AI should never make up a number or give a fire probability. If two experiments measured oxygen in different ways, the site won't put them on the same chart. When there isn't enough data to answer something, it says so. The rankings are meant for research, not as safety advice.

Tools

HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Python, Netlify, Google Gemini API, Playwright for testing, and GitHub. We used Claude as a coding assistant.
